rewrites.blindSummary:
The country presents real, structured danger for trans visitors — institutionalised, presidential-level hostility that has become government policy. Police profile and detain trans women for identity checks (20 detained in the largest city in July 2025), trans women have historically been frequent targets of torture and ill-treatment by police, and a trans woman attacked with a knife was herself detained (victim-criminalised). Transphobic attacks and Pride-event violence are documented, and foreign visitors must carry original passports at all times — creating outing risk at the frequent transit checkpoints. A draft law leaked in October 2025 would criminalise LGBT people — not yet passed but under active government consideration. The risk is concentrated in urban trans-visible contexts (districts of the largest city) rather than package-holiday tourist zones, but the institutional hostility pervades.

The consequence axis of an arrest is severe and current: the country holds trans prisoners in gendered facilities by registered sex — a transgender man was held in a women's prison — and a 2024 system-level profile documents LGBTI+ prisoners facing arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation in solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, frequent transfers, and complaints that are ineffective and can lead to further violence, with no policy or staff training to address LGBTI+ needs in a system described as built on a binary, heteronormative model. The December 2025 death of a transgender prisoner in his cell at a women's prison moved the question to formal national-level contestation: rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to “detention practices affecting transgender prisoners,” accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers describe four trans inmates sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, a delayed medical response, investigators entering only two days later and witness statements not taken, and the case was raised in parliament on 12 December 2025. For a trans visitor — already profiled and detained for identity checks — arrest means placement by registered sex in a gendered facility under practices documented as segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched housing, in a system where the most recent custody death is under contested official handling.
rewrites.blindTangential:
The October 2025 draft law is not yet enacted — its status is unresolved and under active government consideration, which colours but does not change a visitor's legal position. The country stands outside the border-control framework of its neighbouring nations, so border and transit controls follow a different regime. A foundational 2008 human-rights report documented a long history of beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people — dated context rather than current street-level risk.

Custody-axis context: the 2024 system-level documentation comes from an international prison profile of the country prepared with a local penal-system association and using regional data, and the December 2025 case's procedural complaints (delayed medical response, late crime-scene entry, witness statements not taken) and the parliamentary question are the formal mechanisms through which trans-prisoner custody conditions are being contested at national level — the death's cause is unresolved and under investigation.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The health ministry is introducing regulations that may profile and restrict trans healthcare — a resident-facing regime; the men's-facility placement of trans women concerns resident detainees. The annual monitoring report records 313 violations in 2025 — roughly two-and-a-half times 2024 — dominated by detention (299 detention decisions), plus systematic privacy attacks; six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings with trans people the most affected, are resident discrimination data, not visitor statistics.

The documented custody practice is resident-facing: trans prisoners held by registered sex in gendered facilities (a trans man in a women's prison), the documented pattern of strip searches, solitary-style isolation, restricted healthcare, frequent transfers and ineffective complaints, and the December 2025 death of a transgender prisoner at a women's prison all concern residents in government custody — a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
The October 2025 draft law is not yet passed — its enactment outcome is unresolved and under active government consideration. General terrorism and crime advisories affect all travellers to the country. No source in the record documents marriage or partner-travel exposure for visitors separately from the general criminalisation risk described above.

Prison axis: no national statute or regulation codifying trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented in this record — the registered-sex placement finding rests on the December 2025 reporting, the segregation-and-isolation practice on the 2024 prison profile, and the December 2025 death's circumstances are contested with the investigation outcome unresolved.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The country demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: a local LGBTI organisation's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022 — hundreds of incidents and dozens of deaths — with 35 victims saying they intended to flee the country. The country's officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds they are not “biological women.” There is no legal gender recognition and no SOGI hate-crime statute (a 2022 law actually increased penalties for “aggravated” LGBT visibility before being struck down).

The national legislature has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives (a 2022 draft bill, later shelved after protests). The community is organised (a local group plus trans collectives) but under pressure. Tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from the general violence level.

The consequence axis if a trans visitor is arrested is documented and dangerous: an international human-rights organisation (7 October 2020) records that the country's authorities facilitate anti-trans violence by placing trans women in men's prisons, exposing them to violence including sexual assault — an activist described her time in a men's prison, saying that at night she was forced to have sex with someone. Placement operated by birth sex in the men's prison system as of 2020, with no gender-identity-based placement policy, no special trans unit, and no trans-specific solitary/segregation practice on record; in a country with no legal gender recognition, a detained trans visitor faces men's-prison placement with documented sexual-assault risk and no documented custody rule or court ruling anchoring a remedy.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Regional legal framework: a 2017 advisory opinion of a regional human-rights court advanced gender recognition in four regional countries, including this one, with compliance still uncertain; a vociferous opposition movement defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash in all four.

Legislative flux: early-2022 bills sought to erase gender-identity protections and restrict legal recognition, and anti-trans initiatives have repeatedly advanced in the national legislature.

The custody finding sits inside a regional and asylum frame: the international human-rights organisation's report documenting birth-sex prison placement is this country's chapter of a three-country report that also examines obstacles to asylum in a neighbouring nation; it documents no trans-specific custody policy or court ruling for this country, and the same report records that the local LGBTI organisation flags forced internal displacement from violence generally — refugee/context material, not a visitor-facing protection.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The femicide-law exclusion of trans women and the absence of legal gender recognition are resident-facing; the documented violence toll — 147 recorded cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders in 2022 (hundreds of incidents, dozens of deaths) — falls on residents.

The organised community (a local group and trans collectives) operates under pressure from the repeated legislative attacks.

Resident custody: the documented practice of placing trans women in men's prisons by birth sex, with sexual-assault exposure (an activist's account), governs residents held in the system, and the local LGBTI organisation flags forced internal displacement of LGBTI people from violence generally — a resident burden; a visitor meets the custody practice only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Unresolved: how the general violence level in communities outside the tourist areas applies to visitors is unquantified — general gang violence affects all travellers, and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from it.

Unverified: no documented trans-visitor incidents appear in the current sources, and the femicide-law exclusion is resident-facing though it signals institutional stance.

Prison axis: the birth-sex placement finding rests on a single international human-rights organisation's documentation (7 October 2020); no national law, regulation, court ruling or custody policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented — in a country without legal gender recognition, that absence cannot be read as a protected standard.
